metadata.title: Artificial intelligence, tasks, skills, and wages: Worker-level evidence from Germany

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses German administrative and survey microdata (BIBB-BAuA 2006/2012/2018 and SIAB 2010–2017) rather than an ILSA student assessment with PVs. For the SIAB wage regressions, the paper describes a 2% random sample of individuals from the German social security system and applies standard wage preparation steps (deflation to base year 2015; imputation for right-censored wages). The methodology does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., sampling weights or replicate weights) in the wage regressions, and the analysis is implemented via fixed-effects Mincer-type regressions with standard errors clustered at the 4-digit occupation level. For the BIBB-BAuA task/skill analyses, the paper mentions inverse sampling weights in robustness figures, but it does not provide a weight variable name or a full weighting protocol for the main regression specifications.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, it models log daily wages and occupational task/skill indicators from German surveys and administrative records. Missing-data handling is therefore not described in the PV sense, and the only explicit missingness-related step concerns right-censored wages in SIAB, which are imputed following Card et al. (2013) rather than through a general missing-data imputation strategy. As a result, the paper does not report a comprehensive missing-data handling method for all variables used in the regressions.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses three German data sources: (i) BIBB-BAuA phone surveys in 2006, 2012, and 2018, restricted to employed people aged 15+ with regular working hours of at least 10 hours per week; task/skill outcomes are 18 task indicators and 8 skill requirement indicators, aggregated to 3-digit ISCO-08 occupations for technology-exposure analyses. (ii) For the wage analysis, it uses SIAB integrated labour market biographies, restricting to full-time workers liable to social security and aged 20–60, and focusing on years overlapping with the AI exposure variation (2010–2017). (iii) For robustness/specification variants, it further restricts the SIAB sample to workers who remain in the same 4-digit occupation and/or the same plant, and to workers observed for eight years. The wage outcome is log daily wage deflated to base year 2015, with right-censored wages replaced by imputed wages following Card et al. (2013).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Mincer-type fixed-effects regressions (Table 2): AI-Exposure_t coefficient 0.0162 (SE 0.00234) in Column 2; benchmark Column 1 coefficient 0.00936 (SE 0.00187). One SD increase in exposure (SD=2.07) associated with ~1.96% higher wage (described in text). R-squared ranges 0.893–0.927 across specifications; clustered SE at 4-digit occupation.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SIAB 2010–2017 (Germany) worker-level wage the study leveraged AI exposure (DAIOE) together with worker, plant, occupation, and year fixed effects to predict log daily wages, finding that higher AI exposure is associated with higher wages (e.g., Column 1 coefficient 0.00936 and Column 2 coefficient 0.0162). This indicates that AI adoption may generate productivity/augmentation gains for workers, but the magnitude depends on specification and occupational mobility constraints.

main_findings.performance_metrics: AI subfield regressions (Table 3): largest coefficients for AI-imgrec_t 0.0694 (SE 0.0439) and AI-stratgames_t 0.0924 (SE 0.0573) and AI-translat_t 0.0422 (SE 0.0208); smallest for AI-readcompr_t 0.0192 (SE 0.00967) and AI-videogames_t −0.00824 (SE 0.0199). R-squared ~0.948–0.950 across columns; clustered SE at 4-digit occupation.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SIAB 2010–2017 (Germany) wage the study leveraged AI subfield exposure measures (DAIOE sub-indices) alongside worker, plant, occupation, and year fixed effects to predict log daily wages, finding heterogeneous wage associations across AI areas (e.g., positive for image recognition and strategy games, negative for video games). This indicates that policy and training should target the specific AI capabilities being adopted rather than treating AI exposure as a single uniform shock.

main_findings.target_variable: Log daily wage (low vs high task churning occupations)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Task-churn splits (Table 4): Panel A (low task churning) AI-Exposure_t coefficients positive across specifications (e.g., Column 1 0.00526; Column 3 0.0162; Column 6 0.0191). Panel B (high task churning) shows positive coefficients in less restrictive samples (e.g., Column 3 0.0153) but negative coefficients under the most restrictive stayers specification (Column 6 −0.0137, SE 0.00666). R-squared ~0.889–0.930; clustered SE at 4-digit occupation.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SIAB 2010–2017 (Germany) wage the study leveraged AI exposure (DAIOE) and occupational task-churning classification together with worker, plant, occupation, and year fixed effects to predict log daily wages, finding that AI is generally wage-positive in low-churn occupations but can be wage-negative for high-churn occupations under restrictive mobility conditions. This indicates that AI’s wage effects depend on how rapidly job tasks change and on workers’ ability to reallocate or adapt, implying that reskilling and mobility support may be crucial in fast-changing occupations.

data.outcome_summary: This paper uses German worker-level administrative data (SIAB) for 2010–2017 to study how occupation-level AI exposure (DAIOE, time-varying) relates to individual wages, alongside descriptive analyses of task and skill changes using BIBB-BAuA surveys (2006/2012/2018). The wage models are Mincer-type fixed-effects regressions with worker, plant, 4-digit occupation, and year fixed effects, and standard errors clustered at the 4-digit occupation level. In Table 2, the benchmark specification shows a positive association between AI exposure and log daily wages; a one-standard-deviation increase in exposure (SD=2.07) corresponds to about a 1.96% wage increase, with coefficients remaining similar under stricter stayers samples. Table 3 demonstrates heterogeneity across AI subfields (e.g., positive for image recognition and strategy games, negative for video games). The study is not an ML prediction paper (no ML algorithms are trained), and causal interpretation is limited because AI exposure is observational and identification relies on fixed effects and controls rather than randomized variation.
